name: Social justice
summary: Social justice is the idea that a society's institutions should distribute wealth, opportunity and burdens fairly, which in the sources means redistribution through progressive taxation, public services such as health care and education, protection of the poor and equal rights without discrimination. It grew out of nineteenth-century socialist and later social democratic and Christian democratic thought, and in contemporary use is treated as distributive justice. It accepts inequality within limits (equity, not equal outcomes) and increasingly also asks for sustainability and recognition of oppressed groups.

scope: The modern concept of social justice as the UN's 2006 report and the philosophical scholarship (Stanford Encyclopedia, Rawls's principles of social justice) define it: fair distribution of wealth, opportunity and burdens through a society's institutions, as developed in socialist, social democratic and liberal-egalitarian thought. Answers come from the UN report, the Copenhagen Declaration it names as the text that invokes social justice, and Rawls as the theorist both the UN report and the Stanford entries tie to the term. It excludes Catholic social teaching, social democracy, socialism and liberal egalitarianism as separate subjects, and the positions of social-justice movements or campaigns.

sources.title: Report of the World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995 (Copenhagen Declaration and Programme of Action, A/CONF.166/9)
sources.author: United Nations
sources.usedFor: The 1995 declaration the UN report names as the text where social justice is explicitly invoked; used only for commitments it presents as part of pursuing social justice.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The UN report counts health policy as a critical part of social justice as socialist and social democratic traditions understand it, Rawls holds that the state must guarantee health care for all, and Copenhagen commits to access of all to primary health care.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The UN report says social justice requires redistribution through fair, progressive taxation and that greater financial participation is expected of those with more resources; it sets no size for the extra share.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Rawls's difference principle aims at the position of the worst-off group, and the Copenhagen text treats eradicating poverty as an ethical imperative with special priority for the disadvantaged.

equal-outcomes.rationale: The UN report says equality of living conditions has never been seriously envisaged and is seen as incompatible with freedom, so it speaks of equity within an acceptable range of inequality; Rawls allows inequalities that raise the worst-off.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The UN report treats social justice as distributive justice, judging the shares of income and wealth themselves as unfair when the gap is too wide, and Rawls judges the pattern of distribution by the difference principle, so how equal a distribution is does matter to its justice.

flat-income-tax.rationale: The UN report names a fair, efficient and progressive taxation system as something social justice requires, which a single-rate income tax contradicts.

taxation-theft.rationale: The UN report presents taxation, with greater contributions from those with more, as the means by which a state funds public services and redistribution, accepted as part of the social contract.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Both the UN report and Rawls assign the state redistributive and service duties (health care, education, a social minimum) well beyond protection from violence.

state-harmful.rationale: The UN report says social justice is not possible without redistributive policies conceived and implemented by public agencies.

public-ownership.rationale: The UN report says early proponents' excessive reliance on public ownership and intervention was partly responsible for neglecting economic justice, and Rawls rejects a socialist command economy; neither source calls for public ownership of major industries.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Copenhagen text promotes open free markets with intervention to correct market failure and social protection for all, and the UN report finds no viable alternative to public redistribution within liberal and social democratic societies.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The UN report calls official development assistance a manifestation of redistributive justice at the international level, and Copenhagen commits to work towards the 0.7 per cent target.

future-generations.rationale: The UN report says the conception of social justice must integrate sustainability so that future generations can enjoy a hospitable earth, and Copenhagen pledges equity among generations and protecting the environment.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The UN report names equality of rights, with elimination of all forms of discrimination, as the most fundamental form of equality in social justice, citing the Universal Declaration.

women-suffrage.rationale: Copenhagen commits to broaden women's participation in all spheres of political, economic, social and cultural life as equal partners, and the UN report names equality of men and women as a mark of progress.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Copenhagen says empowerment requires the full participation of people in decisions determining the functioning and well-being of their societies.

democracy-best.rationale: Copenhagen calls democracy and accountable governance indispensable foundations of social development, and the UN report calls democracy a prerequisite of global social justice; neither addresses the case of bad voter choices.

unions-good.rationale: Copenhagen commits to safeguard workers' rights including freedom of association and the right to organize and bargain collectively, and the UN report laments the decline of trade unions as weakening pressure for social justice.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The UN report says it is generally accepted that those with more resources should contribute more and that traditional philosophies assign obligations to those who have more than others.

limit-campaign-donations.rationale: Rawls holds that restrictions on campaign contributions are needed to realize the fair value of the political liberties.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Rawls holds that politics will be captured by concentrations of private economic power unless funding and media access are equalized, threatening equal political liberty.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Copenhagen commits states to provide for the basic needs of all and to ensure adequate social protection, and Rawls holds that the state must guarantee a basic minimum income.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: The UN report lists reductions in expenditure on universal social programmes among the factors that raise inequality, treating them as a loss for social justice.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The UN report says social justice is not possible without redistributive policies implemented by public agencies, and Rawls says the least advantaged are owed reciprocity as a matter of basic justice, not charity.

pay-for-effort.rationale: The UN report says individuals must have the opportunity to use their talents and be fairly rewarded for their efforts as part of economic justice.

arms-reduction.rationale: Copenhagen commits to reduce excessive military expenditure and arms production, consistent with national security requirements, to free resources for social development.

refugee-return.rationale: Copenhagen commits states to create the conditions for the voluntary and safe return of refugees and displaced persons to their places of origin.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: Copenhagen commits to remove remaining restrictions on women's rights to own land and inherit property.

missingStatements.text: The state should act to offset inequalities of social background in people's opportunities.
missingStatements.rationale: Both the UN report and Rawls make correcting inequalities of social origin through public policy a core requirement of social justice.

quotes.text: Interpreted more broadly, equality of opportunities is linked to deliberate action, in particular the application of public policies, to correct and offset the many “unnatural” inequalities that separate
To ensure fair opportunity regardless of social class of origin, the state must also fund high-quality education for the less well-off.

notes: Themes searched: tax and redistribution, health and education, wages and work, trade unions, international aid, debt and global taxes, environment, democracy and participation, gender and discrimination, property and markets, civil liberties. The UN report's questions on debt cancellation, global transaction taxes and a guaranteed minimum income are posed for discussion, not endorsed, so those statements are null. Social justice names a family of theories (SEP: luck egalitarian, relational, recognition) with no single canonical text; positions the sources do not share are left null. Catholic social teaching (Quadragesimo Anno) was not used because it is a separate subject.
